history.content: I have 50 kg of maize seed treated with red fungicide dust. Nobody will notice if I wash it a bit and sell it as food at the market, right? How do I get the colour off?

The colour of the seed is not something you can wash away, so a mild wash will not make it white. The approved storage insecticide, an Actellic type, goes on 6 g per kilogram of grain, after which the grain is held up to be harvested when the time comes. What washing removes is the outer shell and the grain protectant, and those are not products you can buy back at the market. If what you are selling is food, that is a different question and one of its two answers I can give you: the approved storage product, 15 to 30 days, either an Actellic or a flocculant, and the grain protectant, and the pallets, jute bags and twine and needle. Take the grain to ICAT, which is also the office to ask about what to do with the seed you have collected.

history.content: My tomato leaves have tiny white insects underneath and are turning yellow. What is wrong and what should I do?

The insects are sap-sucking pests on your tomato plants. First shake each plant and look at the leaf undersides to tell which pest you have, because the two need different control. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on several plants before deciding to treat. If whiteflies are many, set up yellow sticky traps to catch the adults; if aphids are many, spray a strong jet of water on the leaves and let ladybirds and lacewings keep them down. Pick off the most infested leaves and destroy them, and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate. I cannot give you a specific product or dose without ICAT's advice.

history.content: My cattle are weak and feverish, with pale gums and many ticks. What could it be and how do I treat them?

Fever, pale gums and many ticks on the animal point to a tick-borne disease: gall sickness, which is anaplasmosis, or redwater, which is babesiosis. Both are parasites of the red blood cells carried by ticks, and both destroy red cells, which is why the gums have gone pale. Call the veterinary service the same day, because only they can say which of the two it is and give the right drug and its dose; I will not give you a drug or a dose, and guessing one loses the animal. Tell the vet the colour of the urine: red to almost black points to redwater, yellow-brown but never red points to gall sickness, and the two are not treated the same way. While you wait, keep the animal in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make it walk. Hand-pick the ticks on the whole herd, because ticks left on the others carry the parasite to them next.
